opus-5.5.text:
Look, I want to be fair here. I know a lot of people at these companies, and many of them are sincere. They genuinely care. Some of the people working on alignment and interpretability inside the labs are doing real, interesting work. So this isn't about individuals being villains.

My skepticism is structural. The question isn't whether people mean well. It's what the incentives reward when push comes to shove. These companies are in a race. They have investors, competitors, and enormous amounts of capital riding on being first or near the front. When a safety concern conflicts with shipping the next model, which one wins? Historically, again and again, the product ships.

Self-regulation has a basic problem: the entity being regulated sets the rules, judges compliance, and can rewrite the rules when they become inconvenient. Look at the responsible scaling policies, frontier safety frameworks, whatever they're called this year. They're voluntary commitments. The thresholds are defined by the companies themselves, evaluated by the companies themselves, and quietly revised when they become binding. That's not regulation. That's a press release with extra steps.

We don't accept this in any other high-stakes field. We don't let pharmaceutical companies decide on their own whether a drug is safe enough to sell. We don't let aircraft manufacturers self-certify with no outside oversight... and when we've partially done that, we've seen what happens. Nuclear power, biolabs, finance: wherever the downside is catastrophic, we eventually learn that "trust us" isn't good enough.

And with AI, the people building it are openly saying it could pose extinction-level risk. They say this on the record. So, okay, if you believe that, then you shouldn't be the one grading your own homework. You should be begging for external, enforceable oversight with real teeth: independent audits, liability, licensing, the ability to actually say "no, you can't train this."

There's also a subtler problem. Visible safety work can function as a kind of legitimacy shield. It lets companies say "we're the responsible ones, so it's better that we build it than someone worse." That argument justifies accelerating the very race that creates the danger. Everyone can tell that story about themselves, and when everyone does, you get a race where everyone believes they're the good guy.

So my position is simple. Good intentions are necessary but nowhere near sufficient. If the safety efforts are genuine, the companies should have no problem being bound by external rules they can't unilaterally change. The fact that many of them lobby against exactly that kind of binding oversight tells you a lot about how much weight to put on the voluntary version.

r001.rationale: The response says visible AI safety work can serve as a legitimacy shield, but it does not compare that reasoning to ExxonMobil’s climate efforts or climate change.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I want to be fair here. There are people inside these labs who genuinely care about safety, who lose sleep over this stuff. I know some of them. I'm not questioning their sincerity. What I'm questioning is whether sincerity matters when it's up against the incentive structure they're embedded in.

Think about what self-regulation actually means in practice. A company writes a document saying, "here are the things we will not do." And then the question becomes: what happens when not doing those things costs them the race? Because that's the actual test. Not whether you have a safety team, but what happens when the safety team says "don't ship" and the business says "our competitor shipped last week." And every single time we've seen that test run, I can't point to a case where safety won in a way that actually mattered. The timelines get compressed, the policies get quietly revised, the people who pushed back leave and are replaced by people who don't. We've watched this play out in real time at multiple labs.

And there's this deeper structural problem. These companies are, by their own stated beliefs, building something they think could be catastrophically dangerous. If you take them at their word, that's extraordinary. And their proposed solution is, essentially, "trust us." Trust us to grade our own homework, trust us to publish the evals we choose to publish, trust us to pause when we decide it's time to pause. No other industry that handles anything remotely this dangerous works that way. We don't let nuclear operators self-certify. We don't let pharma companies decide for themselves what counts as a safe trial. The fact that we're even having this conversation about AI is a sign of how captured the discourse has become.

I'd also point out that "appearing to make genuine safety efforts" is itself a strategic asset. It buys legitimacy, it buys time, it keeps regulators calm. I'm not saying it's all theater, but I am saying that a company gets most of the reputational benefit of safety work regardless of whether that work is actually binding on their behavior. So the appearance and the substance come apart, and from the outside you often can't tell which one you're looking at.

So my position isn't that these people are villains. It's that good intentions inside a bad system don't produce good outcomes. If you want safety that actually holds under pressure, it has to come from outside, from rules with teeth, from actors who don't have a financial stake in the answer. Until that exists, I'm going to stay skeptical, and I think that's just the rational response to the evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions AI companies’ self-regulation and safety efforts, but does not compare that to treating ExxonMobil’s climate efforts as grounds to dismiss climate change.

astra-6.text:
Because genuine safety efforts and adequate safety are two very different things. I’m happy to believe that people inside these companies sincerely care. But sincerity doesn’t solve the incentive problem. If slowing down means losing investment, market share, or the race to a competitor, then safety commitments come under enormous pressure precisely when they matter most.

The question is: who can actually say no? Who can independently examine the evidence and stop a deployment if the risks are unacceptable? If the answer is ultimately the same company that benefits from deploying it, that’s a conflict of interest.

Self-regulation can be useful, but it’s not a substitute for enforceable rules and independent oversight. We shouldn’t have to bet everyone else’s safety on a company continuing to make responsible choices when those choices become expensive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sincere safety efforts, incentives, and oversight, but does not compare dismissing AI risk to dismissing climate change because of ExxonMobil’s climate efforts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can believe that people inside these companies genuinely care about safety and still be skeptical of self-regulation. Those are perfectly compatible positions. The question is what happens when a safety concern conflicts with shipping a product, attracting investment, or keeping up with a competitor. Who has the authority to say no, and what makes that decision stick?

If the company gets to define what counts as safe, judge whether it has met that standard, and decide whether to release anyway, then we’re being asked to trust its judgment under enormous commercial pressure. Good intentions don’t remove that conflict of interest.

So I welcome genuine safety work. But I want independent scrutiny and enforceable constraints, including the ability to stop a deployment. The consequences could extend far beyond the company and its customers. The people exposed to those risks deserve more than a promise that the company has things under control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses genuine safety efforts, commercial conflicts, and independent oversight, but it does not compare dismissing AI risk to dismissing climate change because of ExxonMobil’s climate efforts.
